Where it began

Jack Hobbs came into the world in Cambridge on 16 December 1882. He was mad about cricket early, playing in the streets near home and watching the college matches around the town. His real classroom was Parker's Piece, a stretch of open common where he practised whenever work allowed. He trained as a gas fitter, and for some years nothing marked him out.

Then, in 1901, something clicked. He made his first hundred, local sides took notice, and Tom Hayward, the Surrey and England batsman and a Cambridge man himself, came to watch him bat on the Piece. Surrey took Hobbs on in 1903, and once he had qualified he made 88 on his first-class debut in 1905 and a hundred in his next game.

The player

His Test debut came at Melbourne on 1 January 1908, and he made 83 in his first innings. Two winters later in South Africa he worked out the googly bowlers who had baffled almost every other English batsman, and made his first Test hundred, 187. In Australia in 1911–12 he scored 662 runs in the series, a record at the time, and he and Wilfred Rhodes put on 323 for the first wicket. No pair had added more for any wicket in a Test, and that stand stood as the record for 22 years.

In all he played 61 Tests between 1908 and 1930, making 5,410 runs at 56.95 with 15 hundreds and 28 fifties. His best was 211 against South Africa at Lord's in 1924. When he left the game in 1934 he had made 61,760 first-class runs and 199 centuries, more than anyone before him.

What made him special

Hobbs had quick feet, a stroke for most deliveries and a gift for steering the ball where the fielders were not. He was often at his best when the pitch was at its worst. He loved a quick single, and his opening stands with Rhodes, Andy Sandham and above all Herbert Sutcliffe were built on sharp running. With Rhodes he barely needed to call. In Tests he and Sutcliffe opened together 38 times and averaged 87.81 a stand.

He could field, too. On that 1911–12 tour he ran out 15 batsmen from cover point, and the Australians learned not to run on him. Bowling was a gentler story: one Test wicket in 61 matches, at 165 runs apiece. Some jobs are best left to the specialists.

Away from the middle

Wisden made him one of its Cricketers of the Year for his 1908 season, and much later one of its five Cricketers of the Century, alongside Don Bradman, Garfield Sobers, Shane Warne and Viv Richards. In 1953 he was knighted, the first professional cricketer to be given the honour. He opened a sports shop in London and kept it going for most of the rest of his life, and after he stopped playing he wrote about the game as a journalist.

And finally

In 1923 he reached his hundredth first-class hundred. Only W. G. Grace and Tom Hayward had got there before him. That was rather fitting company: the grand old champion of the game, and the man who had once come out to Parker's Piece to watch a young Cambridge lad bat.
